1.open: When something at home or work is falling apart, who or what do you count on to hold things together?
questions: Paul says he thanks God because he has heard of "your faith in Christ Jesus and your love for all the saints" (v. 4). He had never even met them. What do you think people hear about your church or your group, and what would you like them to hear?

Paul prays that they would be filled "with the knowledge of His will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding" (v. 9). Why do you think he connects knowing God's will with how we actually live (v. 10)?
Verse 13 says God "has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of His beloved Son." What does it mean to you to be rescued, as opposed to simply improved?
Verse 15 says, "The Son is the image of the invisible God." If someone asked what God is like, how might Jesus help you answer? If you are not sure God is like that, what gets in the way?
Paul says "in Him all things hold together" (v. 17). Where in your life right now does it feel like things are coming apart, and what would it look like to bring that to Jesus?

Many Christians read "firstborn over all creation" (v. 15) as a title of rank, while some groups read it as meaning the Son was the first being created. How do you hear the rest of verses 15 to 20 shaping the way you read that phrase?

Verses 21 and 22 say we were once "alienated from God" but are now reconciled, to be presented "holy, unblemished, and blameless." How does it feel to hear that described as something Christ has done rather than something you have to earn?

Verse 23 speaks of continuing "in your faith, established and firm." What helps you keep going when faith feels shaky, and what makes it harder? Feel free to answer honestly, including if you are struggling right now.
1.life: Pick one thing in your life that feels like it is coming apart. Each day this week, name it to God in a sentence and say "in Him all things hold together" (v. 17) as you hand it over.
1.prayer: Thank God for rescuing us and bringing us into the Son's kingdom. Pray for the group by name, asking that each person would grow in the knowledge of God and have strength to keep going.
1.tip: Verses 22 and 23 can sound to some people like their standing with God depends on their performance. Read them slowly and point out that the whole passage rests on what Christ has already done (vv. 13, 14, 20, 22), and that holding steady is the response of someone who has been rescued. Give anxious people room to say so without rushing to fix it.

2.open: What is a rule from your family or childhood that you still follow today, even though nobody makes you?
questions: Paul says he is struggling for people who have not met him face to face (v. 1). Who is someone you care about but rarely see, and what does caring for them look like?
Paul wants them "knit together in love" (v. 2). What helps a group of people become close like that, and what gets in the way?
In verse 6 Paul says, "just as you have received Christ Jesus as Lord, continue to walk in Him." What was your own starting point with Jesus, and what has helped you keep walking since?
Paul warns against being taken captive "through philosophy and empty deception" (v. 8). What ideas today sound wise or deep but leave people empty?
Verse 10 says, "you have been made complete in Christ." Where do you catch yourself feeling that something is still missing, and what do you reach for to fill it?
Verse 14 pictures the record of our debt as "nailing it to the cross." What does it mean to you that the charges against us are taken away, and is that easy or hard to believe?

Verses 16 and 17 say no one should judge you over food, festivals or the Sabbath. Christians read this differently, some saying those laws no longer apply and others saying only that we shouldn't judge one another over them. How can people in the same church hold different views and still treat each other well?

Paul says rules like "Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch!" have "an appearance of wisdom" but are "of no value against the indulgence of the flesh" (vv. 21, 23). Where have you seen strict rules fail to change a heart, and what do you think does change it?
2.life: This week, notice one moment when you feel you have to earn God's approval or measure up to someone else's standard. Stop and remind yourself out loud that in Christ you have been made complete (v. 10), then ask God to help you rest in that.
2.prayer: Thank God that in Christ we have everything we need and that our debt has been taken away. Ask for help to stop judging others and to stop trying to prove ourselves.
2.tip: Verses 16 to 18 can pull the group into an argument about the Sabbath, food laws or angels. Name once that Christians disagree, then steer back to Paul's main point: Christ is enough. Give quiet people room to say where they feel they fall short without being fixed.

3.open: What is one piece of clothing you keep wearing long after you should have thrown it out?
questions: Paul says, "your life is now hidden with Christ in God" (v. 3). What do you think it means that your life is hidden, and how does that sit with you on an ordinary Tuesday?
Verse 2 says to "set your minds on things above, not on earthly things." What does your mind tend to return to when nothing is demanding your attention?
Verse 5 calls greed "idolatry," and verse 8 adds anger, slander and "filthy language." Which of these is easiest for us to excuse in ourselves, and why?
Paul talks about taking off the old self and putting on the new, like changing clothes (vv. 9, 10). Where do you feel like you are still halfway between the two?

Verse 11 says "Christ is all and is in all," with no Greek or Jew, slave or free. Who are the people today that we are tempted to rank above or below others, and what would it look like to treat them as Paul describes?
Verse 13 says, "Forgive as the Lord forgave you." Is there someone you find it hard to forgive? If you would rather not name anyone, what makes forgiveness hard in general?
Verse 15 says, "Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts." What does it look like when peace is in charge, and what usually competes with it for the job?

Verses 18 to 25 give instructions to wives, husbands, children, fathers and slaves, and Christians read them differently today. Which part do you find hardest to read, and what do you notice about the duties given to those with more power, like husbands and fathers (vv. 19, 21)?
3.life: Pick one item from Paul's clothing list in verse 12: compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness or patience. Each day this week, look for one chance to put it on with someone close to you, and notice what happens.
3.prayer: Thank God that your life is held safe with Christ. Ask for help to take off one old habit and to put on love, especially with the people nearest to you.
3.tip: Verses 18 to 25 can take over the whole evening. Say plainly that Christians disagree on how verse 18 applies today, and that slavery was never something to defend; then steer back to the chapter's main thread, which is a new life shaped by Christ's love. Be sensitive that someone in the room may have been hurt by how these verses were used.

4.open: Who is someone you always look forward to hearing from, and what makes their messages or calls special?
questions: Paul tells masters to give their slaves "what is right and fair," because they too have "a Master in heaven" (v. 1). Slavery is hard to read about today. How do you respond when the Bible speaks to a practice we find troubling, and what do you notice about the way Paul holds owners accountable?
Paul says, "Devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful and thankful" (v. 2). What gets in the way of steady prayer for you, and what has helped, even a little?
Paul asks for prayer that God would open "a door for the word," even though he is "in chains" (v. 3). What does it say about Paul that he asks for open doors and not for release?
Verse 6 says, "Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt." What does speech like that sound like in real life, and where do you find it hardest, at work, at home or online?

Verse 10 asks the church to welcome Mark, who had once left Paul partway through a journey. Why might Paul take the trouble to say this? Where have you seen a second chance given, or needed one yourself?
Epaphras is "always wrestling in prayer" for the Colossians (v. 12). Who has prayed for you in a way you could feel, and who might you pray for with that kind of effort?
Paul fills the end of his letter with names: Tychicus, Onesimus, Aristarchus, Luke, Nympha and more. What does this long list of ordinary helpers tell you about how God's work gets done?

Paul signs off with "Remember my chains. Grace be with you" (v. 18). If you are tired, unsure or just going through the motions in your faith right now, what would you want to say honestly about where you are?
4.life: Pick one person who has been a quiet helper in your life, like Tychicus or Epaphras were for Paul. This week, send them a note or make a call to thank them by name, and tell them you are praying for them.
4.prayer: Thank God for the people who have carried you in prayer. Ask for open doors to share his good news and for words that are "gracious, seasoned with salt."
4.tip: Verse 1 can pull the whole evening into a debate about slavery. Name plainly that it is hard to read, say the group can come back to it, and then keep the focus on Paul's point that every owner answers to a Master in heaven. Save most of your time for the prayers and the people in the second half.
